supported_facts: Forbes published an April 4, 2026 estimate that Steve Witkoff's fortune was about 15% higher than a year earlier, at about $2.3 billion.
Forbes attributed the increase to his World Liberty Financial venture and SpaceX stake; it presented an estimate and attribution, not proof that official acts caused private gains.
unsupported_original_claims: The frozen July 2026 date/window does not match the April 2026 Forbes story.
The reviewed source does not verify that White House divestment assurances remained unresolved through July 2026, nor does it establish that Iran diplomacy benefited Witkoff's portfolio.
access_notes: Forbes article returned readable text excerpts; wealth figures and attribution are explicitly Forbes estimates.
narrow_corrected_title: Forbes Estimates Steve Witkoff's Fortune Rose 15% to $2.3 Billion
narrow_corrected_claim: Forbes estimated on April 4, 2026, that Steve Witkoff's fortune had risen about 15% over the preceding year to $2.3 billion, attributing much of the increase to World Liberty Financial and a SpaceX stake. The estimate does not establish a causal link to his diplomatic work.
exact_remaining_gap: The April Forbes article does not establish the claimed July 2026 divestment status or a connection between diplomatic decisions and personal gains.

supported_facts: Reuters reported that the August 15, 2025 Anchorage summit produced no Ukraine ceasefire.

Reuters on August 16 reported, citing a Financial Times account sourced to people briefed on the talks, that Putin sought Ukraine's withdrawal from Donetsk and offered to freeze other front lines if his terms were met.
unsupported_original_claims: The reviewed reporting does not establish a secret Trump-Putin agreement committing Ukraine to cede Donetsk.
The reporting describes a Russian proposal, not an accepted settlement; the frozen account's characterization of a concluded 'understanding' is unsupported.
access_notes: The supplied Reuters August 15 article URL was not retrievable from the source cache; the Reuters live-update page and August 16 follow-up returned readable excerpts. The follow-up attributes the reported terms to the Financial Times and unnamed sources.
narrow_corrected_title: Trump-Putin Anchorage Summit Ends Without Ceasefire as Donetsk Proposal Is Reported
narrow_corrected_claim: The August 15, 2025 Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage ended without a ceasefire. Reuters later reported, attributing the account to the Financial Times and sources briefed on the talks, that Putin had proposed Ukraine give up Donetsk in exchange for freezing other front lines.
exact_remaining_gap: No public transcript or corroborated record reviewed here establishes a secret bilateral agreement, Trump's assent to Ukraine ceding Donetsk, or Ukraine's acceptance.

supported_facts: KFF's analysis of P.L. 119-21 says states must redetermine Medicaid expansion adults' eligibility every six months for renewals scheduled on or after December 31, 2026.

The law limits retroactive coverage beginning January 1, 2027 to one month before application for expansion adults and two months for other Medicaid applicants; it does not eliminate retroactive coverage.
unsupported_original_claims: The frozen claim that the law ends retroactive Medicaid coverage is false.
The source supports the statutory requirements and effective dates, not the card's unqualified prediction that they will reproduce the prior unwinding's harms.
access_notes: KFF's full article text was retrieved; the relevant sections are 71107 (more frequent eligibility determinations) and 71109 (retroactive coverage).
narrow_corrected_title: 2025 Reconciliation Law Requires Six-Month Medicaid Expansion Renewals and Shortens Retroactive Coverage
narrow_corrected_claim: P.L. 119-21 requires six-month eligibility redeterminations for Medicaid expansion adults for renewals scheduled on or after December 31, 2026. Beginning January 1, 2027, it shortens retroactive coverage to one month for expansion adults and two months for other Medicaid applicants.
exact_remaining_gap: The law's implementation and coverage effects are not established by the statutory summary; do not describe retroactive coverage as abolished or assert a specific realized loss without later evidence.

supported_facts: ProPublica reported that Reyes Holdings benefited from an exemption for PET resin in the 2025 tariff list.
The article reports that Reyes Holdings' owners had donated to Republican causes and that the company hired Ballard Partners to lobby on tariffs; it describes the exemption process as opaque.
unsupported_original_claims: The source does not establish that exemptions were sold or granted in exchange for donations or lobbying.
The supplied ProPublica reporting does not substantiate every separate claim in the frozen synopsis about Apple, an academic 1-in-5 versus 1-in-10 comparison, or the February 2026 senators' letter.
access_notes: ProPublica article text excerpts were retrieved, including its PET-resin and lobbying passages. The article says the role of lobbying in the exemption was unclear.
narrow_corrected_title: Reyes Holdings Benefited From a PET-Resin Tariff Exemption After Lobbying
narrow_corrected_claim: ProPublica reported that Reyes Holdings received a PET-resin tariff exemption after hiring Ballard Partners to lobby on tariffs; the company's owners had donated to Republican causes. The report documents an opaque process and overlapping political connections, but does not prove a quid pro quo.
exact_remaining_gap: The reviewed source does not establish that donations or lobbying caused the exemption or that firms purchased tariff relief.

supported_facts: Reuters reported that Trump's 2025 financial disclosure included $2.8 million in Trump Watches royalties, $2.5 million from sneakers and fragrances, $1.3 million from the Greenwood Bible, and $1.16 million from NFTs.
Reuters said the disclosure appeared largely to cover calendar year 2024.
unsupported_original_claims: The disclosure does not show merchandise sold 'from the Oval Office' or establish that the White House operated the businesses.
The reviewed Reuters reports do not support the frozen synopsis's Gold Card, 21 foreign real-estate projects, or later $1.2 billion annual-income assertions as part of this disclosure.
access_notes: Reuters article excerpts were retrieved and provide the listed amounts; Reuters described the filing's coverage of 2024 as apparent, not definitive.
narrow_corrected_title: Trump's Financial Disclosure Reports Millions in Merchandise Royalties
narrow_corrected_claim: Reuters reported that Trump's 2025 financial disclosure listed millions in royalties from branded goods, including $2.8 million from watches, $2.5 million from sneakers and fragrances, and $1.3 million from the Greenwood Bible. The filing appears largely to cover 2024 and does not establish Oval Office sales.
exact_remaining_gap: The cited disclosure and reporting do not establish where products were sold, that the presidency served as the sales channel, or the separate later-year financial claims in the frozen synopsis.

supported_facts: Talking Points Memo and The Daily Beast reported an account attributed to an anonymous former White House official that Acosta told Trump transition interviewers he had been told Epstein 'belonged to intelligence' and to leave the matter alone.
The cited account is secondhand reporting; it does not itself verify the underlying statement or its truth.
unsupported_original_claims: The frozen synopsis says internal DOJ emails to Geoffrey Berman substantiate the quote; neither reviewed article supplies those emails as proof.
The sources do not establish what Trump personally knew about the alleged statement when he nominated Acosta.
access_notes: TPM and Daily Beast article excerpts were retrieved. They attribute the claim to a former White House official; no internal DOJ email or firsthand transition record was reviewed.
narrow_corrected_title: Reporting Attributes an Epstein 'Intelligence' Explanation to Acosta's Transition Interview
narrow_corrected_claim: In July 2019, The Daily Beast and Talking Points Memo reported an account from a former White House official that Alexander Acosta had told Trump transition interviewers he was told Jeffrey Epstein 'belonged to intelligence' and to leave it alone. The claim remains attributed reporting, not a finding established by the cited articles.
exact_remaining_gap: The cited reporting does not provide contemporaneous DOJ emails, a firsthand public account from the transition interviewers, or evidence of Trump's knowledge of the alleged statement at the time of Acosta's nomination.

supported_facts: The White House published the executive order on January 21, 2025; it revoked Executive Order 11246 and directed a 90-day transition period for federal contractors.
The order directed agencies to enforce federal civil-rights laws and addressed illegal discrimination and preferences.
unsupported_original_claims: The frozen May 15 date is incorrect for this executive order.
The cited order does not establish a May-June expansion abolishing all DEI programs at every contractor and federal grant recipient or a completed shutdown of all such programs.
access_notes: The White House order text was retrieved; the signature date, revocation list, and transition provision appear in the order itself.
narrow_corrected_claim: On January 21, 2025, Trump signed an order revoking Executive Order 11246, the federal-contractor equal-employment and affirmative-action framework, and provided a 90-day transition period. The cited text does not show that every contractor or grant recipient immediately ended all DEI activity.
exact_remaining_gap: The cited order does not support the May 2025 date or establish the scope and implementation of later requirements across all contractors, grantees, universities, hospitals, and research institutions.

supported_facts: Reuters reported that Musk announced the America Party in response to Trump's tax-and-spending bill.
On July 6, 2025, Trump called Musk's proposed party 'ridiculous,' in a further public exchange during their feud.
unsupported_original_claims: The supplied articles do not verify Trump repeatedly using the nicknames 'Baby Elon' or 'Low-IQ Elon'.
The supplied articles do not verify the synopsis's claim that Musk amplified deepfakes and conspiracy theories throughout July and August.
access_notes: Both Reuters reports returned readable excerpts. This proposal uses the specific public exchange they document and omits unverified quotes and conduct.
narrow_corrected_title: Trump Calls Musk's Proposed America Party 'Ridiculous'
narrow_corrected_claim: After Elon Musk announced the America Party in response to Trump's tax-and-spending bill, Trump called the proposal 'ridiculous' on July 6, 2025. The reports document a public dispute, not the unverified nicknames or deepfake claims in the frozen synopsis.
exact_remaining_gap: The reviewed Reuters stories do not establish the claimed exact nicknames, deepfake amplification, or the full duration and prominence of the feud.

supported_facts: Rep. Andy Ogles announced and introduced H.J.Res.29 on January 23, 2025, proposing a constitutional amendment allowing up to three presidential elections.
Congress.gov lists Ogles as the resolution's sponsor and its referral to the House Judiciary Committee on January 23, 2025.
unsupported_original_claims: The resolution was not introduced on August 29, 2025 by a coalition of lawmakers.
The sources establish a proposal, not that lawmakers acted days after the unspecified comments described in the frozen synopsis.
access_notes: Ogles's House press release and the official Congress.gov bill page returned readable text; the bill record lists one sponsor.
narrow_corrected_title: Rep. Andy Ogles Introduces Third-Term Amendment Proposal
narrow_corrected_claim: Rep. Andy Ogles introduced H.J.Res.29 on January 23, 2025, proposing an amendment that would allow a person to be elected president up to three times. Congress.gov lists Ogles as sponsor and referral to House Judiciary; the record does not show a coalition introduction on August 29.
exact_remaining_gap: These sources do not identify a later August 29 coalition event matching the frozen claim.

supported_facts: ODNI announced on July 30, 2025 that DNI Tulsi Gabbard had released documents concerning a whistleblower's account of events preceding the 2017 Intelligence Community Assessment on Russian election interference.
The release presents Gabbard's interpretation and allegations; the announcement is not independent adjudication that the intelligence assessment was fabricated.
unsupported_original_claims: The date and composite description about COVID origins, the Russia investigation, and the 2020 election do not match this July release.
The reviewed release does not substantiate the frozen claims of deliberate selective omission, political motive, or compromised collection methods.
access_notes: The ODNI press release was retrieved in full. It is an official statement by the agency and attributes contested conclusions to Gabbard.
narrow_corrected_title: ODNI Releases Whistleblower Account About the 2017 Russia Intelligence Assessment
narrow_corrected_claim: On July 30, 2025, ODNI said Tulsi Gabbard released documents describing a whistleblower's concerns about the preparation of the January 2017 intelligence assessment on Russian election interference. The release records Gabbard's allegations and the whistleblower account; it does not independently establish them.
exact_remaining_gap: The cited release does not support a March 2025 omnibus event spanning COVID origins, Russia, and the 2020 election or establish the stated motive and downstream effects.
